OUR CIVIL SERVICE AND CRITICISM.
It was the late Sir Henry May—a Colonial Governor of outstanding personality—who—said Hongkong people were never satisfied. It was a war-time utterance. People were getting tired of all of being compelled to trapse to what is now ungraciously called Seven-and-six-penny Hill, to obtain permission to leave the Colony, and later to the Central Police Station for the same purpose. These ungrateful Hongkong people felt, and rightly so, that the Post Office building was a most convenient place to go to obtain the desired permission. This does not prove that the inherent passion of Hongkong people is to criticise unduly the Civil Service—as HE the Governor's remarks would lead the reader to believe—but rather the fact that when criticism of a public nature has been levelled at the action of those in authority there has been

ment. Transposing the word opposition into criticism, and admitting that the regime about to end its days in Hongkong has been of its kind, good, or comparable with others, it must be admitted that a little of its success must be ascribed to the criticism which has been levelled at it. Much of this criticism perhaps has been unnecessary, but that has not been the fault of the Press. The Government has chosen to be silent on many things when a word in season would have meant the necessary, enlightenment. We have not yet reached the age of supermen even though many of our Cadets exhibit feats of versatility. The success of that versatility, we venture to assert, is primarily due to the men under them whose work has become second nature to them. To this great body of public efficiency the highest praise is due. The nature of their service prohibits them expressing opinions. At first sight the prohibition seems harsh. A little consideration will convince that it is wise. But even they must feel that certain things might well have been said and done better. The Press would be traitor to its great inheritance if at times it did not give expression to its views. We repeat that these views have been tempered with sweet reason. The great mass of the people is inarticulate by reason of its somewhat oligarchical form of government. Legislative Councillors are not called to account. If the House of Commons was at one time known as the most exclusive Club in England, it may not be out of the way to describe the Legislative Council. Chamber similarly with regard to Hongkong. ITALIAN OPERA.
SEASON OPENS ON MONDAY.

Owing to steamer delays, the members of the Italian Opera Company will be unable to commence their season on Saturday as previously announced. This is but a pleasure deferred. The Company will perform on Monday the evergreen and popular Rusticana ang Pagliacci. This is a splendid opening and should prove the merits of a company who have had success wherever they have appeared. Musical critics elsewhere speak most highly of the leading members of the Company. Signorina Lida Betti has earned high praise for her singing and acting in "Madame Butterfly" as has also Signorina Lucio Varco. The same has occurred in connection with the opening operas. The other members of the Company are all in the front rank of their profession. Added to this an efficient chorus and orchestra, and it will be seen that Hongkong is in for a decided treat. Booking is at Moutrie's.
RICE FOR JAPAN.

Columbia could not have left well alone in 1402, but of course he was not to live to realise the results of his curiosity that in the twentieth century America would inflict upon a long suffering, peace jaded word cross word / puzzles, Prohibitions jokes, the Ford motor car, and Jazz. The Literary Digest quotes Punch who says that Prof. J. W. Gregory declares that if a widely accepted geological theory is right, America is not where it ought to be. We are quite content, however, says "Punch," to let it remain where it is. So are we, drily, replace the Digest. But for all that, we have the Jazz. STRIKE PICKETS.
Strike pickets are not now in favour in these districts, having been snubbed both by the merchants and the officials appointed by Canton.
At the port of Kungyick, 3,000 tins of kerosine were seized by the strikers. The merchants are alleged to have resorted to force and to have driven away the pickets who returned to Canton to report.

Yesterday the strike pickets at this part were arrested by the Red soldiers from Canton. The military allege that the pickets accepted "squeeze" and are sending those detained for trial at Canton. There have been no pickets here since
The strike by rice mill operatives for higher wages is over having been amicately settled.

A pair of mules hitched to a waggon which was in charge of Sapper Goodman. R.E., took
stampede down Garden Road from the Kennedy Road junction yesterday fore noon.
The mad career of the animals was checked by the waggon striking a tree near the Helena May Institute. A Chinese woman who was standing near the tree was slightly injured.
ANOTHER INJUSTICE.

A complaint that Scots are not being kept by themselves in their own regiments is contained in a letter which Mr. J. B. Couper, Unionist M.P. for Maryhill (Glasgow), has sent to the Secretary for War Sir L. Worthington-Evans, on behalf of the St. Andrew Society. The society objects to the anglicisation of Scottish units, and draws particular attention to the case of the Royal Scots Greys, whose depot has been removed from Edinburgh to Canterbury, and of the Cameronians (Scottish Rifles), who according to Mr. Couper, have not only been de- barred from recruiting in their own particular district of Lanark-shire and restricted to London and United but have also had the gates of their own depot at Hamilton placarded with invitations to recruits to join the Irish Guards. The War Secretary has pre- nised to look into the matter on his return from holiday.
